d: New York runs on momentum. Five boroughs, hundreds of neighbourhoods and a transit system that never fully sleeps make it the benchmark for big-city energy. Visitors come for the skyline and the museums; newcomers stay for the career density and the sheer range of food, culture and people within a single subway ride.
h: Central Park and the Upper West Side
bt: April–June and September–November, when walking the city is comfortable.

d: Los Angeles is less a single city than a sprawl of distinct towns stitched together by freeways, beaches and mountains. Sunshine dominates the calendar, entertainment and design drive the economy, and the food scene reflects one of the most diverse populations anywhere. Picking the right neighbourhood matters more here than almost anywhere else.
bt: March–May and September–November; summers inland run hot.

d: Chicago pairs world-class architecture with a Midwestern ease that surprises first-time visitors. The lakefront path, the river and the elevated trains frame a city of strong neighbourhood identities. Housing costs sit well below the coastal giants, which makes it a steady favourite for people relocating for work.
h: Neighbourhood food in Pilsen and Logan Square
bt: May–October; winters are long and windy.

d: Miami is a bilingual, sun-driven gateway between North and Latin America. Beaches and nightlife draw tourists, while finance, tech and trade have pulled in a wave of new residents. Weather is the headline: warm all year, with a wet, humid season that every newcomer should plan around.

Compact, hilly and famously foggy, San Francisco packs a lot of personality into a small peninsula. Its neighbourhoods each have their own microclimate, and the wider Bay Area remains a global centre for technology and venture capital. Layers are mandatory: a sunny morning can turn cool and grey by the afternoon.
h: Golden Gate Bridge and the Presidio
bt: September–October, often the warmest and clearest months.

d: Toronto is Canada's largest city and one of the most multicultural places on the planet. A dense downtown, a lakefront under steady redevelopment and an endless list of neighbourhood food streets define daily life. It is a magnet for newcomers to Canada, which makes rentals competitive and planning ahead essential.
bt: May–October; winters are cold but well served by indoor paths.

d: Montréal blends European street life with North American scale. French is the everyday language, festivals fill the summer calendar, and the city has a reputation for creative industries, universities and relatively affordable rents compared with other major Canadian cities. Winters are serious, and locals embrace them.
h: Old Montréal and the Old Port
bt: June–September for festivals; December–February for winter culture.

d: Vancouver sits between ocean and mountains, so outdoor life is part of the daily routine. The seawall, nearby ski hills and mild winters make it one of the most liveable cities on most rankings, although housing costs are among the highest in North America. Rain is frequent from autumn to spring.

Mexico City is a high-altitude megacity with deep history and a fast-moving creative scene. Leafy districts such as Roma and Condesa have become popular with remote workers, while the historic centre and museums anchor the visitor experience. Altitude, air quality and the rainy-season afternoons are worth watching day to day.

São Paulo is South America's business engine and one of its largest cities. It rewards curiosity: world-class restaurants, a busy arts calendar and distinct neighbourhoods make up for the traffic. Most visits are for work, but many stay for the culture and the food.
bt: April–September, when it's drier and milder.

d: Buenos Aires mixes grand boulevards, café culture and late nights. Neighbourhoods such as Palermo and San Telmo each have their own feel, and the city has long attracted remote workers and long-stay visitors. Currency and prices can move fast, so checking current conditions before you commit is essential.

London is a global capital of finance, culture and education built on a patchwork of villages. Many of its major museums are free to enter, the parks are vast, and the transport network reaches deep into the suburbs. Weather changes fast, so a live forecast check is part of the local routine.
bt: May–September for long daylight; shoulder seasons for value.

d: Paris is compact, walkable and organised into twenty arrondissements that spiral out from the Seine. Café terraces, markets and museums shape daily life, and the city's bike and metro networks make it easy to cover ground. August is quieter for locals, while spring and autumn bring the best walking weather.

Berlin is spacious, green and shaped by its 20th-century history. A strong start-up scene, international population and famous nightlife keep it popular with young professionals and creatives. Each district, or Kiez, has its own rhythm, so where you live defines your Berlin.

Amsterdam is a canal city built for bicycles and short distances. English is widely spoken, international companies are common, and the housing market is tight, which makes early planning important for anyone moving here. Wind and quick showers are part of everyday life.
bt: April–May for tulips; June–August for long evenings.

d: Barcelona combines beaches, distinctive architecture and a strong Catalan identity. The grid-planned Eixample, the medieval Gothic Quarter and hillside parks sit within easy reach of each other. Popular with remote workers and students, it rewards anyone who learns the local rhythm of late lunches and later dinners.

Rome layers nearly three thousand years of history into everyday streets. Ancient ruins, Renaissance squares and neighbourhood trattorias share the same blocks. Summers are hot and crowded, so the city shines brightest in spring and autumn, when walking from site to site is a pleasure.

Lisbon is a sunny, hilly capital on the Tagus estuary that has become a favourite for remote workers and start-ups. Trams, viewpoints and tiled façades give it a strong visual identity, while beaches are a short train ride away. Rising rents mean comparing neighbourhoods carefully is worth the effort.

Istanbul spans two continents across the Bosphorus and has been a crossroads of empires for centuries. Ferries double as commuter transport and sightseeing, and the city's markets and food culture are legendary. It is large and busy, so choosing a base close to the ferry lines saves real time.

Dubai is a fast-built global hub for trade, aviation and tourism. A large international workforce, tax-friendly policies and huge investment in infrastructure attract professionals from everywhere. Summer heat is intense, so life moves indoors and into the evening for several months each year.

Cairo is the largest city in the Arab world and the gateway to ancient Egypt. The Nile, historic Islamic Cairo and the pyramids at Giza draw visitors, while the city itself is loud, warm and full of street life. Traffic is notorious, so timing trips across town matters.

Cape Town sits beneath Table Mountain with two oceans and wine country on its doorstep. It is one of the most scenic cities anywhere and increasingly popular with remote workers in the southern summer. Wind, known locally as the Cape Doctor, can shape the day's plans.

Nairobi is East Africa's business and tech hub, with a national park right at the edge of the city. Its high altitude keeps temperatures mild despite sitting near the equator. A growing start-up scene and regional headquarters make it a frequent relocation destination.
bt: June–October and January–February, the drier months.

d: Mumbai is India's financial capital and home of its film industry. Seafront promenades, colonial-era architecture and some of the country's best street food sit alongside intense density and ambition. The monsoon from June to September transforms the city and reshapes daily schedules.

Delhi is India's capital region, layering Mughal monuments, colonial avenues and modern business districts. The metro makes getting around far easier than it once was. Air quality varies sharply by season, which is exactly why live monitoring matters here.
bt: October–March; check air quality in early winter.

d: Bengaluru is the centre of India's technology industry, with a mild climate thanks to its elevation. Parks, a lively café and craft-brewery culture, and a large young workforce define the city. Commutes can be long, so living near your workplace makes a big difference.

Colombo is Sri Lanka's commercial capital on the Indian Ocean coast. Colonial buildings, new waterfront developments and a relaxed seaside pace sit side by side, and the beaches along the west coast are a short drive away. Two monsoon seasons influence the weather through the year.

Singapore is a city-state known for efficiency, greenery and hawker food. It is a regional base for many multinationals, and its public transport and safety are consistently rated among the best anywhere. Expect warm, humid days year-round with sudden tropical downpours.

Kuala Lumpur offers big-city comforts at a lower cost than many regional peers. A skyline of towers, a diverse food scene and good-value housing make it popular with expats and remote workers. Afternoon thunderstorms are a regular feature of the tropical climate.

Bangkok is a sprawling, energetic capital of temples, markets and rooftop bars. Its street food is world-famous, and skytrain and metro lines make much of the city easy to reach. Heat, humidity and seasonal air quality are the conditions to watch.

Tokyo is vast yet remarkably orderly, a network of neighbourhoods each with its own character. Punctual trains, safe streets and an extraordinary food culture make it a favourite for first-time and repeat visitors alike. Seasons are distinct, from spring blossoms to humid summers.

Seoul blends palaces and mountain trails with cutting-edge technology and fast-moving pop culture. The subway is excellent, cafés are everywhere, and nightlife runs late. Seasonal dust and fine particles in spring make air-quality checks part of daily planning.

Hong Kong squeezes a dramatic skyline between harbour and hills. Hiking trails start minutes from towers, ferries cross Victoria Harbour constantly, and dim sum is a daily institution. Typhoon season from summer to autumn can disrupt plans, so live alerts matter.

Shanghai is China's most international city, combining the historic Bund with the futuristic towers of Pudong. Tree-lined former concession streets offer cafés and boutiques, and the metro network is one of the world's largest. Summers are hot and humid, with a rainy season in June.

Sydney is built around one of the world's great harbours, with surf beaches minutes from the city centre. An outdoor lifestyle, strong job market and sunny climate draw newcomers, though housing is expensive. Summer UV levels are very high, so a daily UV check is a smart habit.
h: Sydney Opera House and the harbour

d: Melbourne is known for laneway cafés, live music, sport and a strong arts scene. Trams criss-cross the city, and neighbourhoods such as Fitzroy and St Kilda each offer a distinct vibe. The weather is famously changeable, sometimes running through several seasons in one day.
